afd.text:
000
FXUS65 KPSR 201825
AFDPSR

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Phoenix AZ
1125 AM MST Tue Oct 20 2026

.UPDATE...Updated Aviation Discussion.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...

- A Pacific low pressure system will bring multiple rounds of 
  showers and thunderstorms, mainly across central and eastern 
  Arizona, Wednesday and Thursday.

- A Flood Watch is in effect across much of south-central and eastern
  Arizona from Wednesday afternoon through Thursday evening for 
  periods of moderate to heavy rainfall leading to flash flooding.

- Quieter weather is expected beginning Friday and lasting through 
  the upcoming weekend.  

- Temperatures through Wednesday will be near to slightly above
  normal before cooling to below normal levels takes place by the
  end of the week and lasts through the weekend. 

&&

.SHORT TERM /Today through Thursday/... 
A very active period is shaping up during the middle portion of 
the week as a strong Pacific low pressure system affects the 
Desert Southwest, bringing multiple rounds of showers and 
thunderstorms. Latest water vapor satellite imagery as well as 
objective analysis show the aforementioned low pressure system 
centered off the northern CA coast early this morning. The low 
pressure system is expected to continue to dive southward and set 
up off the southern CA coast by this evening. In the meantime, an 
upper-level shortwave that was responsible in sparking scattered 
convection yesterday across the southeastern half of AZ is 
already lifting away from the region with weak subsidence 
overhead. Therefore, conditions for today should remain relatively
quiet with dry conditions prevailing across the region with the 
only exception being near the vicinity of the White Mountains 
where the combination of sufficient mid-level moisture and 
orographic lift will likely spark a few afternoon showers and 
thunderstorms. With upper-level heights rising ahead of the 
digging Pacific low, afternoon high temperatures today will be a 
few degrees above normal as many of the lower desert communities 
top out around 90 degrees.

As the Pacific low positions itself off the southern CA coast later 
this evening, the flow aloft will become established more out of the 
south. This will result robust moisture advection with PWAT values 
by early Wednesday morning expected to approach 250-300% of normal 
and will be near record levels for mid-October. There will also be a 
shortwave out ahead of the main Pacific trough that will traverse 
the region early Wednesday morning, which may spark areas of 
showers, especially across the higher terrain areas. Otherwise, the 
main period of impactful weather is likely to occur from Wednesday 
afternoon through Thursday. Latest guidance continues to show 
moderate instability building across much of south-central and 
eastern AZ Wednesday with MLCAPE values approaching 1000 J/KG. This 
amount of instability combined with abundant moisture will yield a 
favorable environment for thunderstorms to produce heavy rainfall 
rates in excess of 1-2"/hr with training of activity likely to occur 
and thus heightening the potential for flash flooding. Latest hi-
res guidance shows activity developing Wednesday afternoon across 
higher terrain areas east of Phoenix before activity develops into
the south-central AZ lower deserts heading into Wednesday evening
and continuing into the overnight and morning hours of Thursday 
as the main upper-level jet streak energy approaches, resulting in
strong divergence aloft. The period between Wednesday evening 
through Thursday afternoon will likely be the timeframe with the 
greatest threat for widespread heavy rainfall and thus flash 
flooding. Latest WPC QPF depicts total rainfall amounts of 
1.50-2.50" across the foothills and higher terrain areas north and
east of Phoenix while across the lower deserts, average rainfall 
amounts will remain under an inch. However, even across the lower 
deserts, especially with any training of activity, there will be 
the potential for areas to receive locally higher rainfall amounts
in excess of 1". In coordination with the neighboring offices, a 
Flood Watch has been issued across much of south-central and 
eastern AZ. 

In addition to the heavy rainfall and flash flood threat, another 
threat to watch out for will be severe weather. Given the moderate 
levels of instability in place combined with strong 0-6 km vertical 
shear in excess of 50 kts, the thunderstorms that do develop will 
likely have some organization to them with the potential to acquire 
supercellular characteristics. In fact, the Storm Prediction Center 
has highlighted much of the higher terrain areas east of Phoenix in 
a slight risk (Level 2 out 5) for severe weather for Wednesday, with 
a marginal risk (Level 1 out 5) across the rest of south-central AZ, 
including the Phoenix metro area. The thunderstorms that do develop 
will be capable of producing damaging wind gusts, large hail, and 
even an isolated tornado given that there will be about 10-20 kts of 
low-level shear. The threat of severe weather will also exist into 
Thursday as well, especially Thursday morning, as the instability 
and shear parameters will still be sufficient. 

As the upper trough gradually pushes inland through the southern 
Great Basin during the day on Thursday, strong dry air advection 
will gradually spread from west to east with rain chances ending 
late Thursday afternoon across the south-central AZ lower deserts 
and likely take until late Thursday night into early Friday 
morning for rain chances to end across the higher terrain areas. 

With the main trough axis still remaining far enough west on 
Wednesday, afternoon high temperatures will still be near normal as 
readings top out in the mid to upper 80s. As the main trough axis 
pushes inland through the southern Great Basin on Thursday, 
temperatures will be noticeably cooler with afternoon highs topping 
out in the low 80s across the south-central AZ lower deserts to low 
to mid 80s across the western deserts. Depending on the amount of 
cloud cover and rainfall activity, there is the potential that 
temperatures in south-central AZ turn out to be cooler than what is 
currently forecasted.

&&

.LONG TERM /Friday through Monday/... 
Much quieter weather is expected starting Friday with much drier 
air in place behind the departing trough. Another follow-on 
shortwave is likely to dive in from the northwest late Friday into
Saturday with guidance indicating that this shortwave will become
a cutoff low over AZ as it detaches from the main jet stream 
energy. At this time, this feature is likely to be inconsequential
given that there will be an abundance of dry air in place 
limiting any additional rainfall potential. Under the general 
troughing influence, afternoon high temperatures through the 
upcoming weekend will remain below normal. Coolest day is expected
on Friday when much of the lower deserts struggle to reach 80 
degrees for afternoon highs. 

&&

.AVIATION...Updated at 1825Z.

South Central Arizona including KPHX, KIWA, KSDL, and KDVT: 
The primary aviation weather concern will be the potential for
showers and thunderstorms Wednesday. Guidance continue to suggest
the development of showers and a few isolated thunderstorms
between 06Z-12Z overnight tonight. Uncertainty in this activity
impacting the terminals remains, with PROB30s in place. The
primary impacts with this would be briefly lowered visibilities
and erratic wind directions. Expect SCT-BKN cloud bases to lower
to around 6-8 kft and may stick around throughout the morning and
afternoon Wednesday. Thunderstorm chances increase at the end of 
the period with some potentially becoming strong to severe.

Outside of any thunderstorm impacts, winds will favor a southerly
crosswind component this afternoon, becoming light and variable
this evening through the overnight hours. Speeds will mostly
remain aob 10 kts.

Southeast California/Southwest Arizona including KIPL and KBLH:
No aviation weather concerns are anticipated through the next 24
hours. Winds at KIPL will favor the S-SE, while directions at KBLH
favor the S-SW. Speeds will mostly remain aob 10 kts with light
and variable winds occurring throughout the period. Cloud bases,
becoming SCT-BKN at times, will remain aoa 7 kft.

&&

.FIRE WEATHER...
Wind speeds today will generally remain light with limited
afternoon gustiness before increasing towards the middle of the
week ahead of an approaching weather system. Mainly dry conditions
will prevail today before rain chances increase substantially
Wednesday and Thursday with significant rainfall amounts, in
excess of 1.00", likely across the higher terrain areas of the
eastern districts. MinRHs today will range between 30-50% before
increasing above 50-60% across the eastern districts Wednesday and
Thursday along with good to excellent overnight recoveries. 
Temperatures will be in a near normal range during the next couple
of days before falling into a below normal category by the end of
the week and lasting through the weekend. 

&&

.PSR WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
AZ...Flood Watch from Wednesday morning through Thursday evening for 
     AZZ545-547-552-556>558-560>563.

     Flood Watch from Wednesday evening through Thursday afternoon 
     for AZZ534-537-538-540>544-546-548>551-553>555.

CA...None.
&&

$$

SHORT TERM...Lojero
LONG TERM...Lojero 
AVIATION...Smith 
FIRE WEATHER...Lojero
